World.title: Call for MH17-style international probe into Zomi Frankcom killing
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Call for MH17-style international probe into Zomi Frankcom killing Matthew Knott August 26, 2026 — 4:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia, the United Kingdom and Canada should consider launching an MH17-style joint criminal investigation into the fatal Israeli drone strike that killed aid worker Zomi Frankcom and her World Central Kitchen colleagues in Gaza, some of the nation’s top international law experts have argued. The Israel Defence Force’s military advocate general last week cleared the military personnel involved in the 2024 drone strike of criminal wrongdoing, infuriating the Albanese government. The UK, Canada and Australia branded the decision not to pursue criminal charges “shameful” in a joint statement over the weekend. “The victims of this incident and their families deserve justice and accountability, and we will continue to seek answers on their behalf,” the nations said. Australian Zomi Frankcom was killed in an Israeli air strike in April 2024.



As well as Frankcom, the seven aid workers killed in the attack included humanitarians from the United Kingdom and a dual Canada-US national. Don Rothwell, an international law expert at the Australian National University, pointed to the joint investigation into the downing of MH17 over Ukrainian airspace as a model that could be followed to try to seek accountability over the killing of Frankcom and her colleagues. “That is an example of a precedent that could be applied in the case of alleged Israeli war crimes committed by IDF members if Israel refuses to prosecute the persons involved,” he said. That probe was led by the Netherlands with support from Australia, Belgium, Malaysia and Ukraine. It led to criminal prosecutions in the Netherlands before a Dutch criminal court, trials in absentia of the accused Russian and Ukrainian nationals, and convictions of three people in 2022.



The Malaysia Airlines flight was shot down in July 2014 while in flight from Amsterdam to Kuala Lumpur and travelling over eastern Ukraine, where separatists backed by Russia were fighting Ukrainian forces following the Russian invasion of Crimea. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Israel could pay reparations to Zomi Frankcom’s family after Australian anger While the Australian Federal Police could launch its own war crimes investigation, Rothwell said a joint probe could provide cover at a time the Australia-Israel relationship is at a “deeply low ebb”. “Australia would feel more comfortable at a diplomatic and political level joining with other nations to seek justice and accountability rather than going it alone,” he said. The material gathered during former defence force chief Mark Binskin’s 2024 probe into Israel’s response to the drone strike could be used for the inquiry, Rothwell said.



Ben Saul, the Challis Chair of International Law at the University of Sydney, said there were “definite advantages” to the idea of launching a joint investigation, including greater resources and sources of intelligence. While the nations would face a formidable task to extradite any soldiers or officers from Israel, he said launching an external investigation would send an important signal to Israeli soldiers that they were not above the law. Staggeringly few Israeli soldiers are ever charged with wrongdoing let alone convicted in the Israeli military justice system, Saul said. The Frankcom family said they were “deeply disappointed” by the military advocate general’s decision and urged the Australian government to “pursue all available legal avenues for an independent and credible investigation to be conducted”. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Foreign Minister Penny Wong branded Israel’s decision an “outrage” and said they would consult the Frankcom family on next steps.



The Israeli military investigation “determined that, notwithstanding serious failures in the process that led to the assessment that Hamas operatives were travelling in the vehicles, the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”. In his 2024 inquiry, Binskin found the strike on the aid convoy was the result of a failure of Israeli military controls “leading to errors in decision-making and a misidentification”, and that the strike violated the Israeli military’s standard operating procedures and rules of engagement. He found the strike “was not knowingly or deliberately directed against” the World Central Kitchen convoy, but called for an official apology to Frankcom’s family. Israeli ambassador Hillel Newman has floated the idea of Binskin returning to Israel to follow up his initial investigation, and said compensation could be paid to the Frankcom family following an official request. “Israel is open to discussions on the legal aspects,” Newman said last week.



“We can share information with legal teams of Australia, and the aspect of reparations can be checked, definitely.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Qantas doubles points, status ahead of credit card changes
World.content:
Travel newsAir travel Qantas doubles points, status ahead of credit card changes Chris Zappone August 26, 2026 — 12:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Qantas is dangling a fresh loyalty offer weeks before new rules are expected to put a dampener on consumers’ frequent flyer activity. From Wednesday until September 2, Qantas frequent flyers will be given double points, or double status credits, for any marketed flight. Qantas’ double points offer can also be applied to Qantas Hotel and Holiday bookings. Dedicated frequent flyers can also earn double status credits, which allow members to scale the frequent flyer tiers (bronze, silver, gold, platinum) faster, giving access to lounges and other perks. The offer comes just over a month before October 1 regulations by the Reserve Bank kick in. Already, the rules are prompting banks to offer fewer points on credit card sign-ups or on spending. (Banks typically purchase the points from airlines, funded in part by transaction fees which the RBA is eliminating).



Some Qantas frequent flyers wait for these specials, which happen once or twice a year, and make multiple bookings, allowing them to lock in their status credits (300 for silver, 700 for gold). The double points can also be applied to Qantas Hotel and Holiday bookings, providing an extra boost for those planning their next getaway, the airline said. 



Eliseo said it’s possible Qantas will reveal the start date for the change at the full-year results. Related Article Opinion

Travel tips What most people don’t understand about frequent flyer bookings Chris Chamberlin Million-mile flyer RBA changes are expected to alter the loyalty industry playing field further, spurring more activity at the retail level. Last week, CommBank unveiled its Yello rewards scheme, where points are earned from every-day spend and redeemed across a range of products, like shopping, gift cards and points transfers to airlines. CommBank’s partner is Virgin’s Velocity program. David Parsons, the chief executive of customer loyalty program consultancy Ellipsis, described the loyalty devaluations triggered by the RBA as “the biggest modern reset” of credit card and airline loyalty schemes. Parsons envisions a split in the market with smaller merchants retaining savings from not paying merchants fees, while Woolworths’ and Coles’ retail programs “keep investing and absorb the attention and spend that will depart from credit card loyalty”.



At the same time, “the airlines lose the daily reinforcement of a co-branded card tap”. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Batman socks, a dog fountain, a cafe corner: Quiet tributes for two fallen officers
World.content:
The police officers who went to Dezi Freeman’s remote home in Victoria’s high country to serve a warrant a year ago today say they didn’t know what they were walking into. But they knew they had two of their best officers with them. Veteran detective Neal Thompson was on his last proper job just days away from retiring while rising star, 35-year-old Vadim de Waart-Hottart, had recently arrived from Melbourne’s Public Order Response Squad. Neal Thompson (left) with his beloved dog Jimmy who passed away only months before the shootings, and Vadim de Waart-Hottart with the painting done for him by someone he helped on the job. In the ambush that followed, Freeman shot both officers dead, and injured another, before disappearing into the wilds of Mount Buffalo in Porepunkah. The murders sparked Australia’s biggest-ever manhunt, ending in Freeman’s death in a shootout seven months later and more than 100 kilometres away at the New South Wales border, and left a community – and two police families – devastated. On Tuesday, hundreds gathered outside the pair’s station in Wangaratta as police unveiled two memorials for Thompson and de Waart-Hottart, hewn from rock side by side. A dog fountain is coming too, for Thompson the dog-lover. And another plaque will be unveiled, further up the mountain in Bright, a year on from the killings on Wednesday.



Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush said it would be “a solemn day for every single member of Victoria Police”. Ten officers went to Freeman’s off-grid property that day to “hold an alleged paedophile to account” as part of a child sexual abuse investigation, Bush said. “Over the last 12 months I have witnessed our organisation unite in times of utter shock and grief, all while remaining steadfast in finding answers for our beloved colleagues.” Mike Bush at the service at Wangaratta police station on Tuesday to unveil memorials for Neal Thompson and Vadim de Waart-Hottart. Joe Armao Many of those answers are still to emerge, ahead of inquests into both the August 26 shootings and Freeman’s final shootout with police when he refused to surrender in his shipping container hide-out near the border. The hunt is still on too for those who helped him on the run, after all those long months of searching and hundreds of police raids across the high country. But this week is not about Freeman, the sovereign citizen lionised by conspiracy theorists online. Nearby towns are heaving with loved ones of de Waart-Hottart and Thompson travelling up for the memorials.



Both men – two toweringly tall cops known for their love of adventure and compassion on the job – were adored not just by friends, but by former partners, as family. WhatsApp groups of ex-girlfriends, united by the tragedies, have been pinging with old photos and favourite memories. In one photo, Vadim holds a painting created for him by someone he helped on the job through a mental health crisis; tall Vadim in a swirl of chaos, listening with his hands clasped. A cloth Batman badge with the Belgium flag designed to honour Vadim de Waart-Hottart by his colleagues. Since his death, some of his former squad mates have taken to wearing a uniform not strictly police-issue: Batman socks and badges. De Waart-Hottart once joked he’d get thrown out of the police academy for wearing Batman socks, but he loved the caped crusader. His little brother Sacha, back home in Belgium where they’d grown up, had always said Vadim was his hero, his Batman, protecting him and now Vadim was out protecting his community. De Waart-Hottart did it all with a smile, acting commander Peta Barrett said Tuesday. In fact, he could never quite believe his own luck. He was brimming with tales of unexpected opportunities, she said, travel disasters that turned into kind offers of hospitality. His family sometimes joked that whenever they encountered their own good luck, they were “doing a Vadim”.



Last August, Vadim, the gentle giant who leapt out of aeroplanes, skied mountaintops and dived in the deep sea, had been excited to explore the Alpine wilderness on his new secondment in Porepunkah. At Thommo’s favourite cafe, run by close friend Anita Cook, a plaque by the bench on the left now reads “Neal’s corner” for his favourite spot where “he could see all the action”, Cook says. Jason South In a cafe just down the road from Wangaratta in Moyhu, a nondescript gold plaque by the bench on the left now reads “Neal’s corner”. This was Thompson’s favourite cafe, run by his close friend Anita Cook. Most mornings, Thompson, or “Thommo” as he was known around town, would slip in early, by the side door, for eggs on the way through from his farm to work, his wire-haired pointer Jimmy at his heels. “He’d always sneak in to surprise me,” says Cook. “He’d have my staff here all intimidated, you know ‘the detective’s in’, but he’d have that smirk. He was a big softie and if you were in, in his circle of trust, he’d do anything for you.” His sisters Dianne Thompson and Lois Kirk, who joined de Waart-Hottart’s aunt at the Wangaratta memorial on Tuesday, said their big brother had followed their grandfather into the police force, and “truly loved his job”. He was “fiercely loyal, a natural leader”, as tough as he was soft.



Thompson’s girlfriend Sergeant Lisa Thompson said every day since losing him had felt surreal. “Nothing will fill the hole Neal’s loss leaves behind, but his stoic words, ‘C’mon, get on with it!’, and the lessons he shared with us, give [us] the strength to keep going,” she said. Thompson was an experienced bushman, who knew the beautiful but treacherous terrain of the wet Alpine valley well. While he was going to miss the job in retirement, he had grand adventures planned too, alongside his best friends Andrew “Crouchy” Crouch and Dirk Wendt. He had some Steve Irwin in him, Wendt says, or perhaps it was the accident-prone Russell Coight – known for his fascination with wildlife and fast MacGyver fixes (including the more-than-occasional stuff up) out in the bush. Thompson’s best friend Dirk Wendt brings his own dog Beau, brother of Thompson’s beloved late dog Jimmy, and Jimmy’s daughter dog Ivy, to visit the new memorial. Joe Armao Thompson’s ex-partner and friend Ange Creighton recalls with fondness the disaster of one of their early dates, a camping trip, when Thommo nearly sank the boat. “Then he wanted me to go rock climbing with him and I thought hmm, maybe not.



As a surprise for Thompson’s upcoming retirement, his station had made special beer stubbies: Thommo immortalised as ‘The Don’ from The Godfather. “But he had this incredible focus with it, like he had with gun safety and especially with his work, too, for all the silly stuff he did out of hours.” Thompson knew Freeman, and had gone along that day to help keep him calm. “He’d have been so careful,” says Creighton. “He was great at building rapport. Quite a few of the local crooks were sad when he died.” His favourite crook even had a nickname for Thommo: “The Don”. As a surprise for his last shift the week of the shooting, Thompson’s police station had made special beer stubbies: Thommo immortalised as ‘The Don’ from The Godfather, with the slicked back hair and a better suit than he’d ever worn himself.



Related Article Good Weekend ‘Thommo’ was days from retirement when he walked into an ambush. Today, his colleagues remember him “As soon as I heard about the shooting, I knew it’d be him,” says Cook, who had served Thommo as usual on his way through her cafe before work that morning. “He was always, you know, send junior to the back, ‘I’ll go in first’.” ”He was, kind of, the man that I’d call on, if I needed anything. Even when he died, he had my steel on the back of his car to take to the wreckers for me. So to not have that ... because you know I’m just on my own.” Bush said that Victoria Police will now “carry forth Neal and Vadim’s legacies for the rest of time”. De Waart-Hottart’s mother Carolina and father Alain said the love for Vadim in his new home of Victoria had brought them immense comfort, including in Porepunkah – a place named for an Aboriginal word meaning the meeting of two rivers.



“Here, at this meeting place, we honour both rivers,” they said in a tribute published in full below. “The river of grief for the life we have lost, and the river of love for the life Vadim gave us.” With John Silvester The Two Rivers Grief is a river that now runs through all our lives, unmapped, shoreless, the nature of mourning. The death of Vadim, our son, Sacha’s brother and your brother in this noble family of blue has brought us together today. For there are now two rivers flowing in our lives connecting us forever.The river of loss and grief and the river of life and love.This river of life is always flowing forwards to join with the vastness of the eternal ocean. So too are we all destined to return to the eternal. No energy is ever lost; it is simply transformed. Death is the only promise held. The transient moving towards the eternalWe have the capacity to hold both emotions:Grief and joy.Sorrow and gratitude.Sadness and happiness.Absence and presence.While we are grieving the trauma of a young life that was taken from us, we simultaneously hold in our hearts our happy memories of his life lived with passion, enthusiasm, generosity and pure love of life with his trademark ever present infectious smile. We also feel gratitude for the life we still have the grace to live now. Grief is not something we can simply choose to leave behind. It is a powerful and overwhelming emotion, and we need to find the grace to flow with it; to allow ourselves to be carried by its current when we need to. But there are moments when we can choose which river we wish to turn towards: the river of grief, which can drag us down into the muddy depths of sorrow; or the river of life, where we can consciously harness the winds and fill our sails with all that is joyous. We cannot stop the river of grief from flowing through us. But we can learn to flow with it, and, when we are ready, to lift our eyes towards the river of life and allow ourselves to be carried forward. When two rivers meet, they merge, blending their distinct waters, each carrying different stories. There are times when the rivers join, as we experience both emotions of grief and love simultaneously. There are times the rivers will part travelling over new terrains.Just like a confluence where two rivers collide, the initial meeting of deep grief is turbulent and churning before it finds a broader, steadier flow. The river does not become wider by forcing one current to disappear. It becomes wider allowing both currents to coexist.As we too must embrace the grief and the love.For I have learnt to see that grief is the mirror of love.We are living in two realities: the physical and the cosmic.It is said that this grief is love with nowhere to go.So let us all give it somewhere to go, let it sense gratitude for what we have. Let the river teach us that we can hold both stillness and storm, flexibility and strength, become a rapid or a quiet reflecting pool.Let the stars remind us that light is revealed in the darkness.To have known the light that is Vadim has brought us all much laughter and kindness. We all now walk the banks of the river of life hand in hand. Our family feel a deep connection and gratitude to all of you here today, one year after Vadim’s departure. We are especially grateful to those who were with Vadim in his final moments on earth, at Porpunkah, the aboriginal word for the ‘meeting of two rivers’. Here, at this meeting place, we honour both rivers: the river of grief for the life we have lost, and the river of love for the life Vadim gave us. And so, as we continue along the river of life, we carry Vadim with us — in our memories, in our love, and in the light he left behind. Two rivers, meeting in one place, flowing together towards the eternal. -De Waart-Hottart family Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Ghislaine Maxwell loses bid to overturn conviction for aiding Epstein
World.content:
New York: Claims by Jeffrey Epstein’s former girlfriend and longtime associate Ghislaine Maxwell that her sex trafficking conviction was a “complete miscarriage of justice” were rejected on Tuesday by a US federal judge who said her assertions were based on “speculation, distortions, and/or outright falsehoods”.

Judge Paul A. Engelmayer said in a written ruling that Maxwell’s habeas petition – a legal procedure challenging her detention – seeking to set aside her conviction and free her from a 20-year prison sentence on the grounds that there was “substantial new evidence” was “demonstrably meritless”.

Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. Getty

“Maxwell’s petition falls very far from the mark,” Engelmayer said. “There is no fact that Maxwell fairly puts in dispute that has any potential to disturb the outcome of her trial.”

Maxwell maintained in a habeas petition last December that information that would have resulted in her exoneration at her 2021 trial was withheld and false testimony was presented to the jury.

World.title: ‘What people don’t realise’: Candid Hird opens up after missing out on the Essendon coaching role
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘What people don’t realise’: Candid Hird opens up after missing out on the Essendon coaching role Jon Pierik Updated August 25, 2026 — 10:47pm ,first published 11:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When James Hird said his goodbyes after finishing his challenging interview before the panel charged with finding Essendon’s new coach, he was buoyant. On two fronts. According to a senior industry figure with knowledge of the Bombers’ interviewing process, the former premiership captain and club great felt as if he had done all he could to reclaim a role he cherished, and one he had held proudly more than a decade ago before trouble struck. Mark McVeigh (left) and James Hird with the Bombers in 2004. Getty Images But, just as importantly, he was also satisfied the Bombers had run a thorough process, where he was given the freedom to push his case, but – on the flipside – was spared no leniency. That’s why, amid the disappointment of being overlooked in favour of great mate Mark McVeigh, Hird cannot complain.



“From a personal point of view though, it’s very disappointing,” Hird said on Nine’s Footy Furnace after it was confirmed that he, like Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham and Adelaide coaching director Murray Davis, had missed out on the job. “Yeah, I’m disappointed, put my heart and soul into the effort, but, obviously, fell short and that’s the way it goes.” Loading On Tuesday night’s episode of Footy Classified (also on Nine), Hird spoke about the Essendon coach selection process and detailed part of an “off-the-record” conversation with club president, and former teammate, Andrew Welsh, who according to Hird told him the process would be genuine, and the Brownlow and Norm Smith medallist was “definitely not at the front of the queue” heading into it. After McVeigh said at his introductory press conference that he loved Hird, and that the two are close friends, Hird expanded further.



“We’ve been friends for 27 years, since he walked in the doors in 1999 to the Essendon Football Club,” he said. “[I’m] incredibly proud of Mark – a wonderful person, great mate, and I couldn’t be prouder. “What people don’t realise is that the last four weeks we’ve been going through this interview process together. We’ve spoken every day over the last four or five weeks about the process, ‘What questions did you get?’, ‘What questions did I get?’ “He’s going to do an incredible job, and I just hope all Essendon people get behind him.” Loading



Before facing the selection committee of chief executive Tim Roberts, Welsh, vice president Anthony Di Pietro, board member and former Swans player Ted Richards and people and culture executive Caroline Monzon, Hird had felt the one issue that may torpedo his bid to return was the hangover from the supplements’ saga all those years ago, the senior industry figure said. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Unite behind our club’: Powerbroker’s call for peace as McVeigh appointed Essendon coach However, Hird felt he had moved on as best he could. McVeigh was one of the 34 players suspended for the 2016 season. Over the years since, Hird has met with many of the 34 who had sought answers, and Hird provided them with as much clarity as he could. There were a couple who still harboured frustration, but Hird, according to the same senior source, had left those deep conversations believing the two parties were now on better terms. This process was relayed to Welsh when he asked Hird about his relationships with those former players, according to the source.



Hird, himself, backed this up on Tuesday night, adding, “some bridges have been mended through the process – some people through the ASADA saga that we sort of headbutted and fought [against], I’ve come back together with them ... there’s been a lot of positives gone on through this process, but as I said it’s time to get behind Mark and the football club and go forward.” Welsh declined to discuss specifics of the interview when asked about this on Tuesday. “I’m not going to go into specifics of candidates. What I will go into is that Murray [Davis], James and Jaymie [Graham] were all fantastic, and all had different views on different things from a game-style perspective, and also from a club perspective, but I won’t be commenting on any questions that we did or didn’t ask any of those candidates,” Welsh said. Hird was pushed and challenged through the Bombers’ detailed process, as were all the candidates. Late in his pivotal interview, Hird, according to two sources with knowledge of the meeting, asked the panel: “What concerns have you got about me being the coach?”



Hird and McVeigh at Essendon in 2010. Getty Images Roberts said he had wondered whether Hird was “bigger than the club”. But Roberts and the rest of the panel agreed in the end that their concerns on that front had been extinguished. Ted Richards, the club’s football director, and a former teammate who went on to be a Sydney Swans’ premiership player, told Hird that successful coaches typically come from a top-four or top-six team and had experience at multiple clubs. Hird did not. Hird politely reminded the questioner that he had been captain of the best team of his era, the dominant 2000 premiership side, and, in his first stint as coach, the Bombers had played off for top spot on the ladder in round 14, 2013. As this masthead has reported, Hird has also made it clear he has been involved in high-performance environments in the years since, including the business world, and you don’t need to follow the “typical linear” model to succeed.



Hird had briefly been an assistant coach at GWS when McVeigh was caretaker coach, and is now director of coaching at VFL club, Port Melbourne. He had seen how the game – and coaching – had changed, the attention span of younger players becoming shorter and shorter in this modern, social media-driven age. Rather than long sermons, Hird had seen the importance of soundbites, and the use of artificial intelligence. Hird was asked how he would handle major media issues. The panel acknowledged that what Hird said, because of his huge standing in the game, let alone the club, carried tremendous weight, so if he broke ranks, the club could be destabilised. Hird responded that he would always consult the president and chief executive, and would fall into line behind what the club wanted, regardless of his own view.



Andrew Welsh (second from left) and McVeigh (second from right) in their playing days. Paul Rovere Soccer great Kevin Muscat was used by the Bombers to scrutinise the applicants’ game plan and strategy, although this was an open-ended question because applicants needed more details on the opponent they may have been playing and conditions at the venue. Related Article AFL briefing

AFL 2026 United Dons vow no ‘jumping at shadows’ now that McVeigh has top job For anyone who has listened to Hird weekly on his football shows on Nine, the owner of this masthead, he has been big on having a team outnumber an opponent at the contest, and then run, spread and attack – as is the modern way. However, Welsh said McVeigh had the better plan. “Mark was clearly the best candidate for what this role demands. He’s developed emerging talent throughout his coaching career, and he connects with younger players in a way that matters for a list at our stage,” Welsh said.



“His game plan is built for the modern game, quick ball movement, adaptable structures, and it’s suited to where this competition is heading.” Hird believed he was the best applicant for the job. As did all the applicants; otherwise, why would they have applied? The Bombers may yet seek to bring him back inside the tent in a prominent role, but Hird craved the senior coaching role, and may be unwilling. Welsh said on Tuesday he was keen to catch up with Hird and would love to see him at Essendon in some capacity. Hird later explained on Footy Classified, “I’ll get round to ringing Andrew, but in my mind there’s no rush, I mean today’s about Mark and about the Essendon Football Club, and what Mark wants to do going forward with the club”. A twist in the tale would be if Hird joined another club, having raised eyebrows on Sunday when he said rivals had reached out to him. Hird has repeatedly said he wants what’s best for the Bombers, a one-time power that has fallen on hard and miserable times and just completed its worst season.



As former club president Lindsay Tanner said, the job of all Essendon people now is to unite behind the new coach. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: No Cripps, no Newcombe: Biggest All-Australian snubs revealed
World.content:
Newly minted All-Australian captain Max Gawn has spoken passionately about the leadership of Jordan Dawson, the Adelaide skipper who gave a spine-tingling speech earlier in the night.

Dawson was named Gawn’s vice-captain in this year’s 23-man All-Australian team. But it was Dawson’s message about the importance of mental health after he tragically lost his older brother Jaryd Dawson during the year that was the most telling.

Jordan Dawson and Max Gawn. AFL Photos

“I think we saw leadership tonight,” Gawn said.

“I think for Jordan to get up and do what he did, to speak about mental health, to lead his side through the tragedy that happened to his family. And then to show vulnerability in front of a group of strangers that he hasn’t got it right, he hasn’t got it perfect with his battle right now, and asking for help – like that’s a captain that I want to be behind.”

The veteran Melbourne captain even half-joked that he was thankful for the “gesture” of being named captain of the AFL’s best team.

“So I appreciate the gesture, but I want to get behind Jordan Dawson, and I want to allow him to do the speech, because his speech was perfect tonight,” Gawn said.

World.title: Call for MH17-style international probe into Zomi Frankcom killing
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Call for MH17-style international probe into Zomi Frankcom killing Matthew Knott August 26, 2026 — 4:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia, the United Kingdom and Canada should consider launching an MH17-style joint criminal investigation into the fatal Israeli drone strike that killed aid worker Zomi Frankcom and her World Central Kitchen colleagues in Gaza, some of the nation’s top international law experts have argued. The Israel Defence Force’s military advocate general last week cleared the military personnel involved in the 2024 drone strike of criminal wrongdoing, infuriating the Albanese government. The UK, Canada and Australia branded the decision not to pursue criminal charges “shameful” in a joint statement over the weekend. “The victims of this incident and their families deserve justice and accountability, and we will continue to seek answers on their behalf,” the nations said. Australian Zomi Frankcom was killed in an Israeli air strike in April 2024.



As well as Frankcom, the seven aid workers killed in the attack included humanitarians from the United Kingdom and a dual Canada-US national. Don Rothwell, an international law expert at the Australian National University, pointed to the joint investigation into the downing of MH17 over Ukrainian airspace as a model that could be followed to try to seek accountability over the killing of Frankcom and her colleagues. “That is an example of a precedent that could be applied in the case of alleged Israeli war crimes committed by IDF members if Israel refuses to prosecute the persons involved,” he said. That probe was led by the Netherlands with support from Australia, Belgium, Malaysia and Ukraine. It led to criminal prosecutions in the Netherlands before a Dutch criminal court, trials in absentia of the accused Russian and Ukrainian nationals, and convictions of three people in 2022.



The Malaysia Airlines flight was shot down in July 2014 while in flight from Amsterdam to Kuala Lumpur and travelling over eastern Ukraine, where separatists backed by Russia were fighting Ukrainian forces following the Russian invasion of Crimea. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Israel could pay reparations to Zomi Frankcom’s family after Australian anger While the Australian Federal Police could launch its own war crimes investigation, Rothwell said a joint probe could provide cover at a time the Australia-Israel relationship is at a “deeply low ebb”. “Australia would feel more comfortable at a diplomatic and political level joining with other nations to seek justice and accountability rather than going it alone,” he said. The material gathered during former defence force chief Mark Binskin’s 2024 probe into Israel’s response to the drone strike could be used for the inquiry, Rothwell said.



Ben Saul, the Challis Chair of International Law at the University of Sydney, said there were “definite advantages” to the idea of launching a joint investigation, including greater resources and sources of intelligence. While the nations would face a formidable task to extradite any soldiers or officers from Israel, he said launching an external investigation would send an important signal to Israeli soldiers that they were not above the law. Staggeringly few Israeli soldiers are ever charged with wrongdoing let alone convicted in the Israeli military justice system, Saul said. The Frankcom family said they were “deeply disappointed” by the military advocate general’s decision and urged the Australian government to “pursue all available legal avenues for an independent and credible investigation to be conducted”. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Foreign Minister Penny Wong branded Israel’s decision an “outrage” and said they would consult the Frankcom family on next steps.



The Israeli military investigation “determined that, notwithstanding serious failures in the process that led to the assessment that Hamas operatives were travelling in the vehicles, the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”. In his 2024 inquiry, Binskin found the strike on the aid convoy was the result of a failure of Israeli military controls “leading to errors in decision-making and a misidentification”, and that the strike violated the Israeli military’s standard operating procedures and rules of engagement. He found the strike “was not knowingly or deliberately directed against” the World Central Kitchen convoy, but called for an official apology to Frankcom’s family. Israeli ambassador Hillel Newman has floated the idea of Binskin returning to Israel to follow up his initial investigation, and said compensation could be paid to the Frankcom family following an official request. “Israel is open to discussions on the legal aspects,” Newman said last week.



“We can share information with legal teams of Australia, and the aspect of reparations can be checked, definitely.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Qantas doubles points, status ahead of credit card changes
World.content:
Travel newsAir travel Qantas doubles points, status ahead of credit card changes Chris Zappone August 26, 2026 — 12:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Qantas is dangling a fresh loyalty offer weeks before new rules are expected to put a dampener on consumers’ frequent flyer activity. From Wednesday until September 2, Qantas frequent flyers will be given double points, or double status credits, for any marketed flight. Qantas’ double points offer can also be applied to Qantas Hotel and Holiday bookings. Dedicated frequent flyers can also earn double status credits, which allow members to scale the frequent flyer tiers (bronze, silver, gold, platinum) faster, giving access to lounges and other perks. The offer comes just over a month before October 1 regulations by the Reserve Bank kick in. Already, the rules are prompting banks to offer fewer points on credit card sign-ups or on spending. (Banks typically purchase the points from airlines, funded in part by transaction fees which the RBA is eliminating).



Some Qantas frequent flyers wait for these specials, which happen once or twice a year, and make multiple bookings, allowing them to lock in their status credits (300 for silver, 700 for gold). The double points can also be applied to Qantas Hotel and Holiday bookings, providing an extra boost for those planning their next getaway, the airline said. 



Eliseo said it’s possible Qantas will reveal the start date for the change at the full-year results. Related Article Opinion

Travel tips What most people don’t understand about frequent flyer bookings Chris Chamberlin Million-mile flyer RBA changes are expected to alter the loyalty industry playing field further, spurring more activity at the retail level. Last week, CommBank unveiled its Yello rewards scheme, where points are earned from every-day spend and redeemed across a range of products, like shopping, gift cards and points transfers to airlines. CommBank’s partner is Virgin’s Velocity program. David Parsons, the chief executive of customer loyalty program consultancy Ellipsis, described the loyalty devaluations triggered by the RBA as “the biggest modern reset” of credit card and airline loyalty schemes. Parsons envisions a split in the market with smaller merchants retaining savings from not paying merchants fees, while Woolworths’ and Coles’ retail programs “keep investing and absorb the attention and spend that will depart from credit card loyalty”.



At the same time, “the airlines lose the daily reinforcement of a co-branded card tap”. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Batman socks, a dog fountain, a cafe corner: Quiet tributes for two fallen officers
World.content:
The police officers who went to Dezi Freeman’s remote home in Victoria’s high country to serve a warrant a year ago today say they didn’t know what they were walking into. But they knew they had two of their best officers with them. Veteran detective Neal Thompson was on his last proper job just days away from retiring while rising star, 35-year-old Vadim de Waart-Hottart, had recently arrived from Melbourne’s Public Order Response Squad. Neal Thompson (left) with his beloved dog Jimmy who passed away only months before the shootings, and Vadim de Waart-Hottart with the painting done for him by someone he helped on the job. In the ambush that followed, Freeman shot both officers dead, and injured another, before disappearing into the wilds of Mount Buffalo in Porepunkah. The murders sparked Australia’s biggest-ever manhunt, ending in Freeman’s death in a shootout seven months later and more than 100 kilometres away at the New South Wales border, and left a community – and two police families – devastated. On Tuesday, hundreds gathered outside the pair’s station in Wangaratta as police unveiled two memorials for Thompson and de Waart-Hottart, hewn from rock side by side. A dog fountain is coming too, for Thompson the dog-lover. And another plaque will be unveiled, further up the mountain in Bright, a year on from the killings on Wednesday.



Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush said it would be “a solemn day for every single member of Victoria Police”. Ten officers went to Freeman’s off-grid property that day to “hold an alleged paedophile to account” as part of a child sexual abuse investigation, Bush said. “Over the last 12 months I have witnessed our organisation unite in times of utter shock and grief, all while remaining steadfast in finding answers for our beloved colleagues.” Mike Bush at the service at Wangaratta police station on Tuesday to unveil memorials for Neal Thompson and Vadim de Waart-Hottart. Joe Armao Many of those answers are still to emerge, ahead of inquests into both the August 26 shootings and Freeman’s final shootout with police when he refused to surrender in his shipping container hide-out near the border. The hunt is still on too for those who helped him on the run, after all those long months of searching and hundreds of police raids across the high country. But this week is not about Freeman, the sovereign citizen lionised by conspiracy theorists online. Nearby towns are heaving with loved ones of de Waart-Hottart and Thompson travelling up for the memorials.



Both men – two toweringly tall cops known for their love of adventure and compassion on the job – were adored not just by friends, but by former partners, as family. WhatsApp groups of ex-girlfriends, united by the tragedies, have been pinging with old photos and favourite memories. In one photo, Vadim holds a painting created for him by someone he helped on the job through a mental health crisis; tall Vadim in a swirl of chaos, listening with his hands clasped. A cloth Batman badge with the Belgium flag designed to honour Vadim de Waart-Hottart by his colleagues. Since his death, some of his former squad mates have taken to wearing a uniform not strictly police-issue: Batman socks and badges. De Waart-Hottart once joked he’d get thrown out of the police academy for wearing Batman socks, but he loved the caped crusader. His little brother Sacha, back home in Belgium where they’d grown up, had always said Vadim was his hero, his Batman, protecting him and now Vadim was out protecting his community. De Waart-Hottart did it all with a smile, acting commander Peta Barrett said Tuesday. In fact, he could never quite believe his own luck. He was brimming with tales of unexpected opportunities, she said, travel disasters that turned into kind offers of hospitality. His family sometimes joked that whenever they encountered their own good luck, they were “doing a Vadim”.



Last August, Vadim, the gentle giant who leapt out of aeroplanes, skied mountaintops and dived in the deep sea, had been excited to explore the Alpine wilderness on his new secondment in Porepunkah. At Thommo’s favourite cafe, run by close friend Anita Cook, a plaque by the bench on the left now reads “Neal’s corner” for his favourite spot where “he could see all the action”, Cook says. Jason South In a cafe just down the road from Wangaratta in Moyhu, a nondescript gold plaque by the bench on the left now reads “Neal’s corner”. This was Thompson’s favourite cafe, run by his close friend Anita Cook. Most mornings, Thompson, or “Thommo” as he was known around town, would slip in early, by the side door, for eggs on the way through from his farm to work, his wire-haired pointer Jimmy at his heels. “He’d always sneak in to surprise me,” says Cook. “He’d have my staff here all intimidated, you know ‘the detective’s in’, but he’d have that smirk. He was a big softie and if you were in, in his circle of trust, he’d do anything for you.” His sisters Dianne Thompson and Lois Kirk, who joined de Waart-Hottart’s aunt at the Wangaratta memorial on Tuesday, said their big brother had followed their grandfather into the police force, and “truly loved his job”. He was “fiercely loyal, a natural leader”, as tough as he was soft.



Thompson’s girlfriend Sergeant Lisa Thompson said every day since losing him had felt surreal. “Nothing will fill the hole Neal’s loss leaves behind, but his stoic words, ‘C’mon, get on with it!’, and the lessons he shared with us, give [us] the strength to keep going,” she said. Thompson was an experienced bushman, who knew the beautiful but treacherous terrain of the wet Alpine valley well. While he was going to miss the job in retirement, he had grand adventures planned too, alongside his best friends Andrew “Crouchy” Crouch and Dirk Wendt. He had some Steve Irwin in him, Wendt says, or perhaps it was the accident-prone Russell Coight – known for his fascination with wildlife and fast MacGyver fixes (including the more-than-occasional stuff up) out in the bush. Thompson’s best friend Dirk Wendt brings his own dog Beau, brother of Thompson’s beloved late dog Jimmy, and Jimmy’s daughter dog Ivy, to visit the new memorial. Joe Armao Thompson’s ex-partner and friend Ange Creighton recalls with fondness the disaster of one of their early dates, a camping trip, when Thommo nearly sank the boat. “Then he wanted me to go rock climbing with him and I thought hmm, maybe not.



As a surprise for Thompson’s upcoming retirement, his station had made special beer stubbies: Thommo immortalised as ‘The Don’ from The Godfather. “But he had this incredible focus with it, like he had with gun safety and especially with his work, too, for all the silly stuff he did out of hours.” Thompson knew Freeman, and had gone along that day to help keep him calm. “He’d have been so careful,” says Creighton. “He was great at building rapport. Quite a few of the local crooks were sad when he died.” His favourite crook even had a nickname for Thommo: “The Don”. As a surprise for his last shift the week of the shooting, Thompson’s police station had made special beer stubbies: Thommo immortalised as ‘The Don’ from The Godfather, with the slicked back hair and a better suit than he’d ever worn himself.



Related Article Good Weekend ‘Thommo’ was days from retirement when he walked into an ambush. Today, his colleagues remember him “As soon as I heard about the shooting, I knew it’d be him,” says Cook, who had served Thommo as usual on his way through her cafe before work that morning. “He was always, you know, send junior to the back, ‘I’ll go in first’.” ”He was, kind of, the man that I’d call on, if I needed anything. Even when he died, he had my steel on the back of his car to take to the wreckers for me. So to not have that ... because you know I’m just on my own.” Bush said that Victoria Police will now “carry forth Neal and Vadim’s legacies for the rest of time”. De Waart-Hottart’s mother Carolina and father Alain said the love for Vadim in his new home of Victoria had brought them immense comfort, including in Porepunkah – a place named for an Aboriginal word meaning the meeting of two rivers.



“Here, at this meeting place, we honour both rivers,” they said in a tribute published in full below. “The river of grief for the life we have lost, and the river of love for the life Vadim gave us.” With John Silvester The Two Rivers Grief is a river that now runs through all our lives, unmapped, shoreless, the nature of mourning. The death of Vadim, our son, Sacha’s brother and your brother in this noble family of blue has brought us together today. For there are now two rivers flowing in our lives connecting us forever.The river of loss and grief and the river of life and love.This river of life is always flowing forwards to join with the vastness of the eternal ocean. So too are we all destined to return to the eternal. No energy is ever lost; it is simply transformed. Death is the only promise held. The transient moving towards the eternalWe have the capacity to hold both emotions:Grief and joy.Sorrow and gratitude.Sadness and happiness.Absence and presence.While we are grieving the trauma of a young life that was taken from us, we simultaneously hold in our hearts our happy memories of his life lived with passion, enthusiasm, generosity and pure love of life with his trademark ever present infectious smile. We also feel gratitude for the life we still have the grace to live now. Grief is not something we can simply choose to leave behind. It is a powerful and overwhelming emotion, and we need to find the grace to flow with it; to allow ourselves to be carried by its current when we need to. But there are moments when we can choose which river we wish to turn towards: the river of grief, which can drag us down into the muddy depths of sorrow; or the river of life, where we can consciously harness the winds and fill our sails with all that is joyous. We cannot stop the river of grief from flowing through us. But we can learn to flow with it, and, when we are ready, to lift our eyes towards the river of life and allow ourselves to be carried forward. When two rivers meet, they merge, blending their distinct waters, each carrying different stories. There are times when the rivers join, as we experience both emotions of grief and love simultaneously. There are times the rivers will part travelling over new terrains.Just like a confluence where two rivers collide, the initial meeting of deep grief is turbulent and churning before it finds a broader, steadier flow. The river does not become wider by forcing one current to disappear. It becomes wider allowing both currents to coexist.As we too must embrace the grief and the love.For I have learnt to see that grief is the mirror of love.We are living in two realities: the physical and the cosmic.It is said that this grief is love with nowhere to go.So let us all give it somewhere to go, let it sense gratitude for what we have. Let the river teach us that we can hold both stillness and storm, flexibility and strength, become a rapid or a quiet reflecting pool.Let the stars remind us that light is revealed in the darkness.To have known the light that is Vadim has brought us all much laughter and kindness. We all now walk the banks of the river of life hand in hand. Our family feel a deep connection and gratitude to all of you here today, one year after Vadim’s departure. We are especially grateful to those who were with Vadim in his final moments on earth, at Porpunkah, the aboriginal word for the ‘meeting of two rivers’. Here, at this meeting place, we honour both rivers: the river of grief for the life we have lost, and the river of love for the life Vadim gave us. And so, as we continue along the river of life, we carry Vadim with us — in our memories, in our love, and in the light he left behind. Two rivers, meeting in one place, flowing together towards the eternal. -De Waart-Hottart family Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Ghislaine Maxwell loses bid to overturn conviction for aiding Epstein
World.content:
New York: Claims by Jeffrey Epstein’s former girlfriend and longtime associate Ghislaine Maxwell that her sex trafficking conviction was a “complete miscarriage of justice” were rejected on Tuesday by a US federal judge who said her assertions were based on “speculation, distortions, and/or outright falsehoods”.

Judge Paul A. Engelmayer said in a written ruling that Maxwell’s habeas petition – a legal procedure challenging her detention – seeking to set aside her conviction and free her from a 20-year prison sentence on the grounds that there was “substantial new evidence” was “demonstrably meritless”.

Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. Getty

“Maxwell’s petition falls very far from the mark,” Engelmayer said. “There is no fact that Maxwell fairly puts in dispute that has any potential to disturb the outcome of her trial.”

Maxwell maintained in a habeas petition last December that information that would have resulted in her exoneration at her 2021 trial was withheld and false testimony was presented to the jury.

World.title: ‘What people don’t realise’: Candid Hird opens up after missing out on the Essendon coaching role
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘What people don’t realise’: Candid Hird opens up after missing out on the Essendon coaching role Jon Pierik Updated August 25, 2026 — 10:47pm ,first published 11:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When James Hird said his goodbyes after finishing his challenging interview before the panel charged with finding Essendon’s new coach, he was buoyant. On two fronts. According to a senior industry figure with knowledge of the Bombers’ interviewing process, the former premiership captain and club great felt as if he had done all he could to reclaim a role he cherished, and one he had held proudly more than a decade ago before trouble struck. Mark McVeigh (left) and James Hird with the Bombers in 2004. Getty Images But, just as importantly, he was also satisfied the Bombers had run a thorough process, where he was given the freedom to push his case, but – on the flipside – was spared no leniency. That’s why, amid the disappointment of being overlooked in favour of great mate Mark McVeigh, Hird cannot complain.



“From a personal point of view though, it’s very disappointing,” Hird said on Nine’s Footy Furnace after it was confirmed that he, like Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham and Adelaide coaching director Murray Davis, had missed out on the job. “Yeah, I’m disappointed, put my heart and soul into the effort, but, obviously, fell short and that’s the way it goes.” Loading On Tuesday night’s episode of Footy Classified (also on Nine), Hird spoke about the Essendon coach selection process and detailed part of an “off-the-record” conversation with club president, and former teammate, Andrew Welsh, who according to Hird told him the process would be genuine, and the Brownlow and Norm Smith medallist was “definitely not at the front of the queue” heading into it. After McVeigh said at his introductory press conference that he loved Hird, and that the two are close friends, Hird expanded further.



“We’ve been friends for 27 years, since he walked in the doors in 1999 to the Essendon Football Club,” he said. “[I’m] incredibly proud of Mark – a wonderful person, great mate, and I couldn’t be prouder. “What people don’t realise is that the last four weeks we’ve been going through this interview process together. We’ve spoken every day over the last four or five weeks about the process, ‘What questions did you get?’, ‘What questions did I get?’ “He’s going to do an incredible job, and I just hope all Essendon people get behind him.” Loading



Before facing the selection committee of chief executive Tim Roberts, Welsh, vice president Anthony Di Pietro, board member and former Swans player Ted Richards and people and culture executive Caroline Monzon, Hird had felt the one issue that may torpedo his bid to return was the hangover from the supplements’ saga all those years ago, the senior industry figure said. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Unite behind our club’: Powerbroker’s call for peace as McVeigh appointed Essendon coach However, Hird felt he had moved on as best he could. McVeigh was one of the 34 players suspended for the 2016 season. Over the years since, Hird has met with many of the 34 who had sought answers, and Hird provided them with as much clarity as he could. There were a couple who still harboured frustration, but Hird, according to the same senior source, had left those deep conversations believing the two parties were now on better terms. This process was relayed to Welsh when he asked Hird about his relationships with those former players, according to the source.



Hird, himself, backed this up on Tuesday night, adding, “some bridges have been mended through the process – some people through the ASADA saga that we sort of headbutted and fought [against], I’ve come back together with them ... there’s been a lot of positives gone on through this process, but as I said it’s time to get behind Mark and the football club and go forward.” Welsh declined to discuss specifics of the interview when asked about this on Tuesday. “I’m not going to go into specifics of candidates. What I will go into is that Murray [Davis], James and Jaymie [Graham] were all fantastic, and all had different views on different things from a game-style perspective, and also from a club perspective, but I won’t be commenting on any questions that we did or didn’t ask any of those candidates,” Welsh said. Hird was pushed and challenged through the Bombers’ detailed process, as were all the candidates. Late in his pivotal interview, Hird, according to two sources with knowledge of the meeting, asked the panel: “What concerns have you got about me being the coach?”



Hird and McVeigh at Essendon in 2010. Getty Images Roberts said he had wondered whether Hird was “bigger than the club”. But Roberts and the rest of the panel agreed in the end that their concerns on that front had been extinguished. Ted Richards, the club’s football director, and a former teammate who went on to be a Sydney Swans’ premiership player, told Hird that successful coaches typically come from a top-four or top-six team and had experience at multiple clubs. Hird did not. Hird politely reminded the questioner that he had been captain of the best team of his era, the dominant 2000 premiership side, and, in his first stint as coach, the Bombers had played off for top spot on the ladder in round 14, 2013. As this masthead has reported, Hird has also made it clear he has been involved in high-performance environments in the years since, including the business world, and you don’t need to follow the “typical linear” model to succeed.



Hird had briefly been an assistant coach at GWS when McVeigh was caretaker coach, and is now director of coaching at VFL club, Port Melbourne. He had seen how the game – and coaching – had changed, the attention span of younger players becoming shorter and shorter in this modern, social media-driven age. Rather than long sermons, Hird had seen the importance of soundbites, and the use of artificial intelligence. Hird was asked how he would handle major media issues. The panel acknowledged that what Hird said, because of his huge standing in the game, let alone the club, carried tremendous weight, so if he broke ranks, the club could be destabilised. Hird responded that he would always consult the president and chief executive, and would fall into line behind what the club wanted, regardless of his own view.



Andrew Welsh (second from left) and McVeigh (second from right) in their playing days. Paul Rovere Soccer great Kevin Muscat was used by the Bombers to scrutinise the applicants’ game plan and strategy, although this was an open-ended question because applicants needed more details on the opponent they may have been playing and conditions at the venue. Related Article AFL briefing

AFL 2026 United Dons vow no ‘jumping at shadows’ now that McVeigh has top job For anyone who has listened to Hird weekly on his football shows on Nine, the owner of this masthead, he has been big on having a team outnumber an opponent at the contest, and then run, spread and attack – as is the modern way. However, Welsh said McVeigh had the better plan. “Mark was clearly the best candidate for what this role demands. He’s developed emerging talent throughout his coaching career, and he connects with younger players in a way that matters for a list at our stage,” Welsh said.



“His game plan is built for the modern game, quick ball movement, adaptable structures, and it’s suited to where this competition is heading.” Hird believed he was the best applicant for the job. As did all the applicants; otherwise, why would they have applied? The Bombers may yet seek to bring him back inside the tent in a prominent role, but Hird craved the senior coaching role, and may be unwilling. Welsh said on Tuesday he was keen to catch up with Hird and would love to see him at Essendon in some capacity. Hird later explained on Footy Classified, “I’ll get round to ringing Andrew, but in my mind there’s no rush, I mean today’s about Mark and about the Essendon Football Club, and what Mark wants to do going forward with the club”. A twist in the tale would be if Hird joined another club, having raised eyebrows on Sunday when he said rivals had reached out to him. Hird has repeatedly said he wants what’s best for the Bombers, a one-time power that has fallen on hard and miserable times and just completed its worst season.



As former club president Lindsay Tanner said, the job of all Essendon people now is to unite behind the new coach. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: No Cripps, no Newcombe: Biggest All-Australian snubs revealed
World.content:
Newly minted All-Australian captain Max Gawn has spoken passionately about the leadership of Jordan Dawson, the Adelaide skipper who gave a spine-tingling speech earlier in the night.

Dawson was named Gawn’s vice-captain in this year’s 23-man All-Australian team. But it was Dawson’s message about the importance of mental health after he tragically lost his older brother Jaryd Dawson during the year that was the most telling.

Jordan Dawson and Max Gawn. AFL Photos

“I think we saw leadership tonight,” Gawn said.

“I think for Jordan to get up and do what he did, to speak about mental health, to lead his side through the tragedy that happened to his family. And then to show vulnerability in front of a group of strangers that he hasn’t got it right, he hasn’t got it perfect with his battle right now, and asking for help – like that’s a captain that I want to be behind.”

The veteran Melbourne captain even half-joked that he was thankful for the “gesture” of being named captain of the AFL’s best team.

“So I appreciate the gesture, but I want to get behind Jordan Dawson, and I want to allow him to do the speech, because his speech was perfect tonight,” Gawn said.

Support is available from Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636 and Lifeline on 13 11 14.

World.title: Government considers effectiveness of teacher education
World.content:
The Education Ministry is considering the effectiveness of teacher education as part of a review of standards for initial teacher education (ITE) providers.

It took over responsibility for the standards from the Teaching Council earlier this year and the Education Minister Erica Stanford has made it clear she expects changes, with repeated statements criticising what she says is the low quality of initial teacher education.

The ministry said nothing had been decided but its review would consider how programmes aligned with curriculum and assessment changes, and how they reflected school and early learning service expectations of new teachers.

It would also improve teacher training so teachers could better meet the needs of disabled students.

The ministry said it commissioned consultants to prepare a discussion document covering "domestic and international evidence on effective initial teacher education and teacher readiness, and identifying areas for further consideration".

University of Waikato Pro Vice-Chancellor Education, Claire McLachlan. Supplied / University of Waikato

Waikato University pro vice-chancellor, education, Claire McLachlan said it was not exactly clear what the minister wanted to change.

"We've got students on campus, we've got them online throughout the country, and we've got them on site in schools. So I have heard her say on radio recently that teacher education is woeful. Which bits are woeful? That's the bit that's unclear to us," she said.

"The universities provide 85 percent of the secondary teacher education programmes, so there's only a small handful of stuff being done by other people. We're doing the bulk of it, so if we're not doing it well enough, then that would be good to know."

McLachlan said Australia went through a similar review over the past five years and she expected similar results - requiring core content on subjects including the science of learning, understanding the role of the brain in learning and knowing how to teach children with diverse backgrounds.

Auckland Primary Principals' Association president Lucy Naylor. Supplied / Milford School

Auckland Primary Principals Association president Lucy Naylor said schools wanted to see more consistency between providers.

"Depending on where your student teacher comes from, the quality of those teachers is very, very varied, extremely varied," she said.

"What they're actually being taught is in some cases, not all cases, inadequate to meet the demands of the new curriculum. So that puts a strain on schools because we are having to do a lot of the training ourselves."

She said some new teachers were graduating with too little classroom experience and welcomed the government's boost to school-based training.

"Teaching is such a relational profession that the biggest, the most positive outcomes we see are from the student teachers who have spent the most amount of time in the classroom during their practicums," she said.

"There are some programmes at the moment where student teachers spend maybe six to eight weeks in a classroom and then off they go. And that's just not good enough."

Howick College principal Dale Burden. Supplied / Howick College

Howick College principal Dale Burden said the government's criticism of universities' programmes was unfair and misplaced.

"Otago University run an absolutely outstanding programme," he said.

"It's a great programme, they're great students, and they make an instant contribution when they come into school."

Burden said the real issue was whether the very best graduates were choosing to become teachers.

"It's about the quality of the students in the programmes. I think that's the thing that really makes or breaks the graduate," he said.

Burden said a bonding scheme succeeded in attracting excellent people to teaching about 40 years ago, many of whom recently retired or were about to.

"That was an outstanding programme, and it captured the best in a generation," he said.

Otago's dean of education Vivienne Anderson. Supplied / Otago University

Victoria University's director of teacher education, Ben Egerton, said it looked like ITE providers were at the start of a period of significant change.

He said they had already altered their programmes to match new teacher standards developed by the Teaching Council and the next target was likely to be greater consistency between the various courses on offer.

"I think it makes sense. We have I don't know how many players in this space nationally, probably 25, 26 tertiary institutions, private providers, polytechnics all offering ITE," he said.

"Having rationalised the teaching standards over the last couple of years for the teaching profession, it makes sense to do this in initial teacher education too."

But Otago University's dean of education Vivienne Anderson said she was worried the government wanted to make system-level changes without good evidence.

World.title: 'Totally wrong': Community up in arms about stormwater runoff into native forest park
World.content:
A community is up in arms over plans to send stormwater runoff into a native forest where an 800-year-old kauri tree lives.

Resource consent has been granted for a housing development near Parry Kauri Park in Warkworth, which allows stormwater from four of the 12 lots to be diverted into the park's stream.

A freshwater ecologist said sending more water into the stream would increase erosion and sediment, harming trees and endangered native creatures.

But Auckland Council said any adverse effects on the park would be minimised.

Volunteer at the park, Nick Sharp, said any more stormwater running into the stream would be bad news for the native forest.

"It's erosion in the creek beds, which then kills all the life in the creek beds. And then eventually trees start falling down as we see in lots of parts of the country. This is totally wrong and what the heck is going wrong?"

Inside the kauri park. RNZ / Luka Forman

The park was bought with money raised by the community in 1965.

It's made up of 8.5 hectares of pristine native bush, which is now administered by Auckland Council, and maintained with the help of volunteers from the Kauri Bushmen's Association.

Freshwater ecologist Sophie Tweddle has been monitoring the stream in the park for the past five years.

Sending more stormwater into the stream would increase sediment and harm at-risk species like longfin eels, giant kokopu, and freshwater crayfish, she said.

"It clogs the gills and the eyes of the animals, it also stops them from feeding because they can't see their prey, it covers the habitat in the stream, so it reduces the amount of places where they can shelter."

Auckland Council had not properly considered how the extra runoff could harm the stream when granting resource consent, Tweddle said.

"It's kind of almost been just shrugged off. They just said 'oh it's going to have no effect'. But actually in a stream like this it could have a massive effect and that should have been considered."

However, Auckland Council's head of resource consents James Hassall said plans for the subdivision would ensure stormwater flow was appropriately managed, and effects on rivers and streams were minimised.

An 800-year-old McKinney kauri. RNZ / Luka Forman

Ray Jensen, who has volunteered at the park for more than 50 years, was concerned about kauri dieback being transported through the runoff from the new subdivision.

Hassall said there was a low risk of that because there were no kauri trees on the development site.

But Jensen worried residents could unwittingly spread it into the stormwater from other forests via their cars or shoes.

"And the trees drinking out of the creek could pick it up. Now these trees - this particular one [the McKinney kauri] has been here for over 800 years and I think it's not our right to kill it."

Sharp believed there was a simple solution to all of this - to divert the stormwater to the north instead.

"Why they never ran it that way I have absolutely no idea because that's naturally where it should flow. About 100 metres of pipe dug up down the side through the development ... would send the water where it should go, away from the park."

He and Jensen recently held a protest on the issue that about 50 people attended.

They contacted the council and local politicians calling for the water be diverted away from the park.

World.title: New Zealand's ATM dead zones
World.content:
New Zealand's network of ATMs has shrunk in recent years, and some parts of the country now do have any cash machines at all.

RNZ research shows there are now just over 1000 access points for cash around the country, at which there may be more than one ATM. About half of the just over 3000 ATMs are owned by non-bank providers.

But there are some places where there is no ATM anywhere near. People living on Great Barrier Island, in Haast, Tuatapere, Omarama and Milford Sound all have to travel a long way to access a cash machine.

From Haast, they might have to drive 144km, from Omarama it is about 30 kilometres to Twizel, and in Tuatapere 48km.

At the Hard Antler Bar and Restaurant in Haast, a staff member said people would get cash out from a local shop or gas station if they needed it. "It would be nice to have one but we manage just fine without. Being so far away from shops we have no need anyway."

In a Haast community group, residents said it was not a huge problem. "If you live off venison, crayfish, veggies from your garden and coffee you don't need any cash," said one.

Others said it was a potential security problem to have an ATM. "ATMs are bad news for small out of the way quiet towns. It puts them in line for serious robbery… plus it requires being topped up a lot which costs a lot which is then passed on to you, the person withdrawing," said another.

Across the country, about 725,000 people live at least 5km from the nearest ATM as the crow flies, 372,162 more than 10km, 200,629 more than 15km and 301 more than 75km.

New Zealand Banking Association chief executive Roger Beaumont said there was a range of factors taken into account when banks were thinking about where to locate ATMs.

"That would probably include things like customer demand for the service, and the practicality of cash in transit services reaching those locations."

The Reserve Bank has been consulting on its plans for cash. It wants 95 percent of people living in urban areas to have walking-distance access to a free cash point.

It has identified 24 rural settlements it says need cash services, including Ngakawau, Ongaonga, Omakau, Owaka, Whangaroa and Taipa, Te Araroa, Cheviot, Rotheram, Waikari, Kimbolton, Kawhia, Balfour, Ohai, Woodlands, St Andrews, Glenavy, Nuhaka, Tuia, Hampton, Kurow, Taharoa, Harihari, Fox Glacier and Ross.

Some of those areas already have limited ATM access.

University of Otago economist Murat Ungor said it was a significant problem that some areas of the country did not have ATMs.

"Research and practical evidence show that people cannot always simply find other solutions, and the burden of doing so falls unevenly on those who are already vulnerable.

"The Reserve Bank has stated that the cash system is not fully meeting the public's needs and that a significant increase in the quantity and quality of cash services is required, especially in rural areas.

"The assumption that people would find other ways is challenged by the realities in these communities. Research shows that 72 percent small businesses would be adversely affected if cash were unavailable. In towns like Palmerston, the only ATM charges a prohibitive $2.80 fee, and businesses have no local way to deposit cash, forcing them to drive long distances, like to Dunedin, just to bank their takings."

He said research focused on rural towns confirmed that declining access was a bigger disadvantage for older people, people who were disabled, on low incomes or with limited transport.

World.title: Government looks to tighten up wholesale investment rules
World.content:
The government is looking to tighten up the rules covering wholesale investment offers, amid concern the current rules are too permissive.

A report by law firm Chapman Tripp says proposed reforms set out in a Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) discussion document could attract "significant industry pushback" particularly on the promotion of wholesale investment offers.

The changes contemplated by MBIE focus on whether:

The eligible investor test is too permissive

The two-year renewal cycle for investor certification is too short

The promotion of wholesale offers to the general public should be more tightly constrained

The various thresholds for wholesale investor status should be adjusted.

Chapman Tripp partner Penny Sheerin said wholesale investment offers were not suitable for inexperienced investors.

"The risk to people offering these deals at the moment is that they have investors who are unsuitable within their investor base, who are really retail investors, who are perhaps inappropriately certifying themselves as eligible investors because they wish to participate in a wholesale offer that may appear attractive to them, but isn't actually suitable for them based on their level of experience in investing," Sheerin said.

The Chapman Tripp report also warned there were risks the regulations could go too far.

"So, for example, I think going too far would be licensing wholesale offerors," Sheerin said.

"That would be something that we wouldn't support, particularly given the global portability of capital and the risk that New Zealand investors may just then simply invest offshore."

The report said some of the reforms could add unnecessary compliance costs.

The partners said concerns about inappropriate advertising of wholesale offers were legitimate, but it was critical that the detailed implementation did not unduly restrict capital-raising in the wholesale sector.

"We are not aware of other countries seeking to licence wholesale offerors and would not support such a move given the global portability of capital and the risk that New Zealand investors may simply invest offshore," the report said, adding there were better ways to manage the risks.

The report said wholesale offers were already under the microscope through the Financial Market Authority's (FMA) recent regulatory proceedings and enforcement actions, with an ongoing focus on wholesale issuer conduct, a thematic review in late 2022, and the High Court judgement concerning eligible investor certificates in late 2025.

World.title: West Coast in for a lashing of heavy rain over next three days
World.content:
MetService says the South Island will bear the brunt of a complex low pressure system which will bring heavy rain to the West Coast over the next three days, from midday Wednesday.

A cold snap was forecast to bring heavy snow to the Canterbury High Country south of the Rangitata River and north of the stretch between Arrowtown and Ranfurly from 6pm, carrying on through until Friday morning.

Rain over the Crown Range Road was also expected to turn to snow on high parts of the road later Wednesday morning.

MetService meteorologist Braydon White said farmers on the eastern side of the divide of the central South Island - including Mount Cook and potentially Twizel - should prepare livestock for a sudden shift from previously warm conditions to a significant amount of snow above 800 metres with lesser amounts forecast to fall as low as 400 metres.

"Going into a much colder situation in the next couple of days, you'll want to make sure that your livestock are doing okay, making sure you have plans in place if you've got any young lambs starting to appear," White said.

He said motorists in the area should consider changing their routes to avoid the higher passes and ensure they had snow chains, sleeping bags, warm clothing, and emergency items with them.

"If you do have to travel, maybe consider having a go bag in your car, just in case you get trapped," White said.

A swollen Twizel River in September 2023. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

Meanwhile, on the western side of the island, a low pressure system - which was travelling down from the east coast of Australia - could see up to 500mm of rain about the Westland ranges with nearly 200mm expected to fall nearer the coast.

The rain was expected to peak at three points across the coming days - reaching up to 30 mm/h on Wednesday afternoon and evening, then again on Thursday evening and in a final burst on Friday morning.
